title: Limb Vessels, Lymphatics & Compartments
summary: Trace the blood and lymph supply of the limbs and see how fascial compartments become clinical emergencies.

lessons.title: Upper Limb Arteries & Collateral Networks

levels.kid:
Your arm is full of tiny pipes that carry blood, like a garden hose system. The big pipe starts near your heart and runs down your arm, changing its name as it goes, the way one road can have different names in different towns.

Near your elbow, the big pipe splits into two pipes that run down to your hand. In your palm, those two pipes join up again in curvy loops called **arches**.

Here is the clever part. Around your shoulder and elbow, there are extra little side roads. If one road gets blocked, blood can take a detour, just like cars going around a closed street. These detours are called **collateral** paths, and they help keep your hand alive and warm.
levels.hs:
**Arteries** carry oxygen-rich blood away from the heart. The upper limb gets its blood from one main vessel that changes name as it crosses landmarks:

- The **subclavian artery** runs over the first rib.
- At the outer edge of the first rib it becomes the **axillary artery** (in the armpit).
- At the lower edge of the teres major muscle it becomes the **brachial artery** in the arm.
- In the elbow pit (the **cubital fossa**), the brachial artery splits into the **radial artery** (thumb side) and the **ulnar artery** (little-finger side).
- In the hand these two join to form the **superficial and deep palmar arches**, which supply the fingers.

A **collateral circulation** is a network of smaller connecting arteries, called **anastomoses**, that lets blood bypass a blocked or tied-off vessel. The shoulder (scapular anastomosis) and elbow both have rich networks.

Real example: the **radial pulse** at the wrist is the pulse you feel when someone checks your heartbeat. Doctors also use the radial artery for arterial blood tests. Before a radial puncture they may do the **Allen test**: they press on both wrist arteries, then release the ulnar one to check that it alone can fill the hand with blood through the palmar arches.
levels.college:
**The axial trunk.** The right subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left directly from the aortic arch. The subclavian artery becomes the **axillary artery** at the lateral border of rib 1, and the axillary artery becomes the **brachial artery** at the inferior border of teres major.

**Axillary artery.** Pectoralis minor divides it into three parts, which give 1, 2 and 3 branches respectively:
- Part 1: superior thoracic
- Part 2: thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic
- Part 3: subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral

The posterior circumflex humeral artery travels with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space.

**Brachial artery.** Its main branch, the **profunda brachii** (deep brachial), runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove. The brachial artery also gives superior and inferior ulnar collaterals. It ends in the cubital fossa, medial to the biceps tendon and deep to the bicipital aponeurosis, by dividing into radial and ulnar arteries, usually at the level of the radial neck.

**Forearm and hand.**
- The **ulnar artery** gives the **common interosseous artery** (anterior and posterior interosseous branches) and mainly forms the **superficial palmar arch**.
- The **radial artery** crosses the anatomical snuffbox, pierces the first dorsal interosseous muscle and mainly forms the **deep palmar arch**. It also gives the princeps pollicis artery to the thumb.

**Collateral networks.**
- **Scapular anastomosis**: suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries (from the subclavian system) link with the circumflex scapular branch of the subscapular artery (from axillary part 3). This network can bypass a gradual blockage between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular origin.
- **Elbow anastomosis**: profunda and ulnar collateral branches link with recurrent branches of the radial, ulnar and interosseous arteries.
- **Palmar arches** connect the radial and ulnar territories.

Clinical point: if the brachial artery must be ligated, tying it off distal to the profunda brachii keeps collateral flow to the forearm.
levels.phd:
Collateral adequacy depends on hemodynamics, not just anatomy. Flow through a collateral bed follows Poiseuille-type behavior: resistance falls with the fourth power of radius. Pre-existing anastomoses therefore carry little flow until a proximal occlusion creates a pressure gradient across them. The rise in shear stress then drives **arteriogenesis**, the remodeling of pre-existing collateral arterioles into larger conduits. Schaper's work showed this process depends on endothelial shear sensing, monocyte and macrophage recruitment (MCP-1), and growth factors such as FGF-2. It differs from **angiogenesis**, the hypoxia-driven sprouting of new capillaries through HIF-1α and VEGF. Because arteriogenesis takes days to weeks, **gradual** occlusion is tolerated far better than acute trauma or embolism. This is why a sudden cut across the axillary artery threatens the limb even though the scapular network exists.

**Developmental variation** explains the high rate of anomalies. The limb axis arises from the seventh cervical intersegmental artery. An early axial artery, continuing as the anterior interosseous artery, is later replaced by radial and ulnar channels. Persistence or abnormal remodeling of these plexiform channels produces:
- **High (proximal) origin of the radial artery**, commonly reported at around 10-15% in cadaver series. The superficial brachioradial variant can be mistaken for a vein.
- **Superficial ulnar artery**, at risk during venipuncture or injection.
- **Persistent median artery**, sometimes contributing to the superficial arch or compressing the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

**Palmar arch completeness** varies. Coleman and Anson's classic dissections (1961) found the superficial arch complete in roughly 79% of hands, while the deep arch is complete in about 97%. Incompleteness reduces the reserve that the Allen test tries to estimate. However, the original Allen test (1929) and Wright's modification have poor sensitivity and specificity against Doppler or plethysmography.

**Subclavian steal** shows collateral physiology in reverse. With proximal subclavian stenosis, the ipsilateral vertebral artery reverses flow and feeds the arm. This is usually silent, but arm exercise can provoke vertebrobasilar symptoms. Scapular collaterals also contribute to flow.
levels.expert:
**Radial access and harvest.** Transradial access is now the default route for coronary angiography in many centers. Large trials such as RIVAL and MATRIX showed fewer access-site bleeds than with femoral access, and MATRIX showed lower mortality in acute coronary syndromes. A key complication is **radial artery occlusion**, which reduces with patent hemostasis and adequate anticoagulation. The **distal radial (snuffbox) approach** punctures beyond the origin of the superficial palmar branch, preserving antegrade flow into the superficial arch. Its proposed advantage is lower occlusion rates, although trial data remain mixed. Radial harvest as a CABG conduit relies on ulnar supply through the arches. RADIAL pooled analyses favor radial grafts over saphenous vein, but Allen-type testing alone poorly predicts hand ischemia, so many teams add Doppler or pulse oximetric plethysmography.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Radial access is increasingly used for neurointerventions such as thrombectomy and aneurysm coiling. Success depends on aortic arch type and on subclavian and vertebral angulation. A high-origin radial artery or radial loop is a common reason for crossover to femoral access, so anatomic variation directly drives procedural planning. Radial artery grafts also serve as high-flow extracranial-intracranial bypass conduits for complex aneurysms.

**Trauma pitfalls.**
- Supracondylar humeral fractures in children can produce a **pink pulseless hand**. Collaterals around the elbow may maintain perfusion despite brachial artery injury or entrapment. Management is debated: many surgeons observe after reduction, while others explore urgently. Concurrent anterior interosseous or median nerve deficits raise concern.
- Axillary artery injury after anterior shoulder dislocation in elderly patients with stiff, atherosclerotic vessels can be masked by palpable distal pulses from scapular collaterals. Diminished pulses are not reassurance.

**Iatrogenic risk.** Accidental intra-arterial injection into a superficial ulnar or superficial brachial artery can cause severe digital ischemia.

**Open questions.** Can therapeutic arteriogenesis be achieved in humans? Growth factor trials (FGF, VEGF, GM-CSF) in limb ischemia were largely disappointing. It is also unclear which bedside test best predicts arch sufficiency, and whether long-term radial access affects future radial graft or fistula options.

keyPoints: Subclavian becomes axillary at rib 1, then brachial at teres major
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts with 1, 2 and 3 branches
Brachial artery splits into radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa
Ulnar mainly forms the superficial palmar arch; radial mainly forms the deep arch
Scapular and elbow anastomoses bypass gradual occlusions via arteriogenesis
Arterial variants and arch incompleteness matter for radial access and harvest

test.q: At which landmark does the subclavian artery become the axillary artery?
choices: Lateral border of the first rib
test.explain: The name changes at the lateral border of rib 1. The axillary artery then becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.

test.q: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
test.explain: Pectoralis minor crosses in front of the axillary artery and is the landmark for its three parts.

test.q: The profunda brachii artery travels with which nerve in the radial groove?
test.explain: The deep brachial artery runs with the radial nerve in the radial groove. The axillary nerve travels with the posterior circumflex humeral artery instead.

test.q: Where does the brachial artery usually divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?
test.explain: The division happens in the cubital fossa, usually at the level of the radial neck.

test.q: Which artery mainly forms the superficial palmar arch?
test.explain: The ulnar artery mainly forms the superficial arch. The radial artery mainly forms the deep arch.

test.q: The common interosseous artery is a branch of the:
test.explain: The ulnar artery gives the common interosseous artery, which divides into anterior and posterior interosseous branches.

test.q: What does the Allen test check?
choices: Whether the brachial artery is narrowed
Whether ulnar flow can supply the hand
Whether the radial pulse is regular
test.explain: With the radial artery compressed, releasing the ulnar artery shows whether ulnar flow through the palmar arches can fill the hand.

test.q: Which vessel takes part in the scapular anastomosis?
test.explain: Suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries link with the circumflex scapular artery around the scapula. The other options belong to the elbow network.

test.q: Ligating the brachial artery is safer distal to the profunda brachii because:
choices: The artery is smaller there and bleeds less
The radial nerve is better protected there
Collateral flow to the elbow is preserved
The ulnar artery begins at that point
test.explain: The profunda brachii feeds the elbow anastomosis, so keeping it allows collateral flow to bypass the ligature.

test.q: Connections between arteries that allow blood to bypass a blockage are called ___.
test.explain: Anastomoses form collateral networks, such as those around the scapula and elbow.

test.q: Name the artery that crosses the anatomical snuffbox.
test.explain: The radial artery crosses the snuffbox and then pierces the first dorsal interosseous muscle to reach the palm.

test.q: The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of the ___ muscle.
test.explain: Teres major marks the transition from axillary to brachial artery.

kidTest.q: What do arteries in your arm carry?
kidTest.explain: Arteries are pipes that carry blood.

kidTest.q: Where does the big arm artery split into two?
kidTest.explain: It splits near the elbow into two arteries that go to the hand.

kidTest.q: What are the curvy loops of arteries in your palm called?
kidTest.explain: The loops in the palm are called arches.

kidTest.q: What happens if one arm artery gets blocked?
choices: The arm grows a new bone
kidTest.explain: Side roads called collateral paths let blood go around the blockage.

kidTest.q: The side-road detours for blood are called c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ paths.
kidTest.explain: Collateral paths are detours that help blood reach the hand.

advancedTest.q: Why is acute axillary artery transection more limb-threatening than slow atherosclerotic occlusion at the same site?
choices: Acute injury destroys the scapular anastomotic vessels themselves
Collaterals need days to weeks of arteriogenic remodeling to enlarge
Slow occlusion triggers VEGF sprouting of large new arteries
Acute injury shifts blood flow toward the vertebral arteries
advancedTest.explain: Pre-existing collaterals carry little flow until shear-driven arteriogenesis widens them, which takes time. Angiogenesis makes capillaries, not large conduits.

advancedTest.q: Distal radial (snuffbox) access is proposed to lower radial occlusion risk mainly because it:
choices: Uses a larger vessel than the forearm radial artery
Lies proximal to the princeps pollicis origin
Stays well clear of the deep palmar arch
Keeps antegrade flow into the superficial palmar branch
advancedTest.explain: Puncture beyond the superficial palmar branch origin preserves forward flow toward the superficial arch, even if the distal segment occludes.

advancedTest.q: A patient with left proximal subclavian stenosis gets dizzy while exercising the left arm. The best explanation is:
choices: Compression of the axillary artery by pectoralis minor
Reversed left vertebral flow supplying the arm
Failure of the superficial palmar arch during exertion
Embolism from the scapular anastomosis to the brain
advancedTest.explain: In subclavian steal, the ipsilateral vertebral artery reverses flow to feed the arm, and arm exercise increases this demand on the vertebrobasilar circulation.

advancedTest.q: An elderly patient has an axillary artery injury after shoulder dislocation, yet the radial pulse is palpable. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
choices: A palpable pulse rules out axillary artery injury
Scapular collaterals may mask a significant arterial injury
Brachial artery spasm has resolved the injury on its own
The ulnar artery has taken over forearm supply
advancedTest.explain: Collateral flow can keep distal pulses present despite axillary injury, so a palpable pulse should not reassure.

lessons.title: Lower Limb Arteries & Pulse Points

levels.kid:
Your blood travels through tubes called **arteries**, like water through garden hoses. One giant hose runs down each leg, all the way to your toes.

At the top of your leg, near the fold where your leg meets your body, the big hose is called the **femoral artery**. Behind your knee it gets a new name. Below the knee it splits into smaller hoses that go to your shin, your calf and your foot.

In some spots the hose runs close to the skin. If you press gently there, you can feel a little tap-tap-tap. That is your **pulse**, your heartbeat traveling down the hose! Doctors feel pulses on the top of the foot and behind the ankle bone. A strong pulse tells them blood is reaching the toes.
levels.hs:
The main artery of the leg starts in the belly. The **aorta** splits into two **common iliac arteries**. Each one divides into an **internal iliac** (supplying the pelvis and buttock) and an **external iliac**, which becomes the leg's main highway.

The route down the leg:
- **Femoral artery**: begins as the external iliac passes under the **inguinal ligament** (the groin crease). Its biggest branch is the **deep femoral artery (profunda femoris)**, which feeds the thigh muscles.
- **Popliteal artery**: the femoral artery passes through a gap in a thigh muscle (the adductor hiatus) and becomes the popliteal artery behind the knee.
- **Anterior tibial artery**: runs down the front of the leg and becomes the **dorsalis pedis artery** on top of the foot.
- **Posterior tibial artery**: runs down the back of the leg, gives off the **fibular (peroneal) artery**, and passes behind the inner ankle bone into the sole.

A **pulse point** is a place where an artery lies near the skin over something firm, so you can feel it beat. The four classic leg pulses are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis.

Example: in a person with diabetes and leg pain on walking, a doctor checks the foot pulses. Weak or absent pulses suggest narrowed arteries, called **peripheral artery disease**.
levels.college:
**Origin.** The external iliac artery becomes the **femoral artery** deep to the inguinal ligament, at the **mid-inguinal point** (halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis). In the **femoral triangle** the order from lateral to medial is nerve, artery, vein, then lymphatics ("NAVeL"). The vessels lie in the **femoral sheath**, but the nerve does not.

**Thigh.**
- Small early branches: superficial epigastric, superficial circumflex iliac, external pudendal.
- **Profunda femoris** arises about 3-4 cm below the ligament. It gives the **medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries** and usually four **perforating arteries** that pierce adductor magnus to supply the posterior compartment. The **medial circumflex femoral** is the main supply to the femoral head.
- The femoral artery continues through the **adductor (subsartorial) canal**, gives the **descending genicular artery**, and exits through the **adductor hiatus** to become the popliteal artery.

**Knee and leg.** The **popliteal artery** is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa. It lies right against the femur and joint capsule, and gives **genicular branches** that form a collateral network around the knee. At the lower border of popliteus it divides:
- **Anterior tibial**: passes above the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment and becomes the **dorsalis pedis** at the ankle.
- **Tibioperoneal trunk**: splits into the **posterior tibial** and **fibular** arteries.

**Foot.** The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into **medial and lateral plantar arteries**. The **deep plantar arch** is formed mainly by the lateral plantar artery and joined by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis.

**Pulse points:**
- Femoral: at the mid-inguinal point.
- Popliteal: deep in the fossa, felt with the knee flexed.
- Posterior tibial: midway between the medial malleolus and the calcaneal tendon.
- Dorsalis pedis: just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon on the dorsum of the foot.
levels.phd:
**Developmental basis.** The embryonic leg is first supplied by the **axial (sciatic) artery**, a branch of the internal iliac. The **femoral system**, arising from the external iliac, later takes over the thigh. The axial artery regresses and persists only in fragments: the inferior gluteal artery, part of the popliteal, and the fibular artery. When it fails to regress, the result is a **persistent sciatic artery** (about 0.025-0.05% of people). This artery is prone to aneurysm and thrombosis. It also produces a confusing exam: the popliteal and pedal pulses are present while the femoral pulse is weak.

**Variation.** The profunda femoris may arise from the posterolateral, posterior or medial wall of the femoral artery. Either circumflex artery may arise directly from the femoral artery, in roughly 15-20% of limbs for the medial one. The dorsalis pedis is absent or not palpable in about 5-12% of normal people. In these cases a large **perforating fibular artery** can supply the dorsum of the foot. So an isolated absent dorsalis pedis pulse is a weak sign of disease.

**Hemodynamics.** Moving away from the heart, the pressure wave is amplified: systolic pressure rises at the ankle while mean pressure falls only slightly. Reflected waves from high-resistance arterioles add to this. It is the basis of the **ankle-brachial index (ABI)**: ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher arm systolic pressure.
- Normal is about 1.0-1.4.
- Below 0.9 indicates peripheral artery disease.
- Above 1.4 means the arteries are stiff and cannot be compressed, typically from medial calcification (**Mönckeberg sclerosis**) in diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Toe pressures are then used instead.

**Collateral networks.** The **cruciate anastomosis** links the inferior gluteal, both circumflex femorals and the first perforating artery. The **trochanteric anastomosis** supplies the hip. The **genicular network** bridges the popliteal artery. These channels allow survival after slow-developing blockages such as atherosclerosis. They do not protect against sudden blockage: popliteal ligation carries a high amputation rate. DeBakey and Simeone's 1946 review of WWII arterial injuries reported amputation in about 73% after popliteal artery ligation, a key argument for vascular repair over ligation.
levels.expert:
**Pulse examination pitfalls.** The examiner may feel their own fingertip pulse. A tachycardic examiner's pulse may be mistaken for the patient's, so compare against the carotid or radial pulse. A palpable pulse does not exclude significant disease, and an absent pedal pulse may be normal anatomy. Handheld Doppler with waveform analysis gives more information: triphasic signals suggest normal arteries, monophasic signals suggest upstream narrowing.

**Trauma.** Knee dislocation injures the popliteal artery in roughly 20-40% of cases, because the artery is tethered at the adductor hiatus and the soleal arch. Pulses may return after reduction and still hide an intimal tear. The standard approach is an **ankle-brachial index** (often called the arterial pressure index in trauma): a value below 0.9 calls for CT angiography or surgical exploration. Hard signs, such as pulsatile bleeding, an expanding hematoma, absent pulses, or a bruit or thrill, mean going straight to the operating room. Warm ischemia lasting more than about 6 hours greatly increases the risk of losing the limb.

**Popliteal pathology.**
- **Popliteal artery aneurysm** is the most common peripheral aneurysm. About half are bilateral, and many patients also have an abdominal aortic aneurysm. These aneurysms cause harm by embolizing or clotting off, rather than by rupturing.
- **Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome** affects young athletes. Abnormal relationships with the medial head of gastrocnemius compress the artery, causing calf pain on exercise. Stress manoeuvres such as active plantarflexion help diagnose it.
- **Cystic adventitial disease** is a rare cause in which a mucin-filled cyst in the vessel wall narrows the artery.

**Procedural anatomy.** The common femoral artery is the default access site for catheter procedures. The ideal puncture lies over the medial third of the femoral head, located with fluoroscopy and ultrasound. Puncturing above the inguinal ligament risks bleeding into the retroperitoneum. Puncturing at or below the bifurcation risks pseudoaneurysm and arteriovenous fistula. The inferior epigastric artery marks the upper limit on angiography.

**Frontiers.** Critical limb-threatening ischemia is now staged with the **WIfI** classification (Wound, Ischemia, foot Infection). The **angiosome** concept targets revascularization to the artery feeding the wound region, although outcome data are mixed. Ongoing research includes deep venous arterialization for limbs with no reconstructable arteries and below-knee drug-coated devices.

keyPoints: External iliac becomes femoral artery under the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point
Profunda femoris supplies the thigh; medial circumflex femoral supplies the femoral head
Femoral becomes popliteal at the adductor hiatus; popliteal splits at the lower border of popliteus
Anterior tibial becomes dorsalis pedis; posterior tibial passes behind the medial malleolus
Leg pulse points: femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis
Ankle-brachial index below 0.9 suggests peripheral artery disease or arterial injury

test.q: The external iliac artery is renamed the femoral artery as it passes deep to which structure?
test.explain: At the inguinal ligament the external iliac becomes the femoral artery, at the mid-inguinal point.

test.q: From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contents are:
test.explain: NAVeL: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics, running lateral to medial.

test.q: Which artery is the main blood supply to the femoral head?
test.explain: The medial circumflex femoral artery, usually a branch of the profunda femoris, is the chief supply to the femoral head.

test.q: Where does the femoral artery become the popliteal artery?
test.explain: After the adductor canal, the artery passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus and becomes the popliteal artery.

test.q: The anterior tibial artery continues onto the foot as the:
test.explain: At the ankle the anterior tibial artery becomes the dorsalis pedis on the dorsum of the foot.

test.q: Where is the posterior tibial pulse best felt?
choices: Between medial malleolus and calcaneal tendon
In front of the lateral malleolus
Lateral to the extensor hallucis longus
test.explain: The posterior tibial artery passes behind the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

test.q: The perforating arteries that supply the posterior thigh arise from the:
test.explain: The profunda femoris usually gives four perforating arteries, which pierce adductor magnus.

test.q: An ankle-brachial index of 0.7 most likely indicates:
test.explain: An ABI below 0.9 suggests narrowed leg arteries. Values above 1.4 suggest arteries too stiff to compress.

test.q: Why is the popliteal artery at particular risk in knee dislocation?
choices: It runs inside the patellar tendon
It is the most superficial structure there
It is surrounded by the femoral sheath
It is tethered and lies against bone and capsule
test.explain: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the fossa. It is tethered above and below and lies against the femur and joint capsule.

test.q: What is the Latin name of the deep femoral artery?
test.explain: The deep femoral artery is called the profunda femoris. It is the main supplier of the thigh muscles.

test.q: The popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal ___.
test.explain: The tibioperoneal trunk splits into the posterior tibial and fibular arteries.

test.q: The posterior tibial artery gives off which artery that runs down the back of the leg near the fibula?
test.explain: The fibular (peroneal) artery branches from the posterior tibial or tibioperoneal trunk.

kidTest.q: What carries blood down to your toes?
kidTest.explain: Arteries are tubes that carry blood from the heart to the body.

kidTest.q: What is the big artery at the top of your leg called?
kidTest.explain: The femoral artery is the big hose at the top of the leg.

kidTest.q: What is the tap-tap-tap you feel when you press an artery?
kidTest.explain: The pulse is your heartbeat moving through the artery.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors feel pulses on your foot?
choices: To check blood reaches the toes
To see how fast you can run
To find out how tall you are
kidTest.explain: A strong foot pulse tells the doctor blood is getting all the way down.

kidTest.q: Your heartbeat that you feel in an artery is called a p _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A pulse is the beat of blood pushed by your heart.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a weak femoral pulse but strong popliteal and pedal pulses. Which anatomy best explains this?
advancedTest.explain: A persistent sciatic (axial) artery comes from the internal iliac and feeds the popliteal artery. The femoral system is often small, so the femoral pulse is weak while distal pulses remain.

advancedTest.q: A diabetic patient with foot ulcers has an ABI of 1.6. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Calcified vessels make the ABI unreliable
Venous disease has raised ankle pressure
advancedTest.explain: An ABI above 1.4 suggests medial calcification (Mönckeberg sclerosis) that resists cuff compression. It can hide true ischemia, so toe pressures are used instead.

advancedTest.q: Why did popliteal artery ligation in WWII cause much more limb loss than slowly developing popliteal blockage?
choices: Collaterals had no time to enlarge
Ligation also damages the tibial nerve
The genicular network is absent in most adults
advancedTest.explain: Collateral networks enlarge gradually with slow occlusion. Sudden interruption leaves an under-developed genicular network that cannot meet the demand.

advancedTest.q: Femoral access puncture is aimed over the femoral head below the inguinal ligament mainly to avoid:
choices: Injury to the medial circumflex femoral artery
Femoral nerve injury and leg weakness
Puncturing the great saphenous vein at its entry
advancedTest.explain: A puncture above the ligament enters a vessel that cannot be pressed against bone. Bleeding then spreads into the retroperitoneum, where compression is impossible.

lessons.title: Superficial & Deep Veins of the Limbs

levels.kid:
Your arteries carry blood out to your fingers and toes. Your **veins** bring it back to your heart. That trip is uphill, especially from your feet!

Your limbs have two sets of veins. Some are **superficial**, just under the skin. Those are the blue-green lines you can see on your wrist. Others are **deep**, hidden between the muscles next to the arteries.

Veins have tiny **valves** inside, like one-way doors. They let blood go up toward the heart but stop it from sliding back down.

When you walk, your leg muscles squeeze the deep veins like hands squeezing toothpaste. That pushes blood upward. It's called the **muscle pump**. So moving around helps your blood get home!
levels.hs:
Blood returns from the limbs through two connected systems of veins.

**Superficial veins** run in the fatty layer just under the skin (the superficial fascia). They don't travel with arteries. **Deep veins** lie beneath the deep fascia, usually running beside an artery of the same name, like the femoral vein next to the femoral artery. **Perforating veins** pierce the deep fascia to link the two systems.

Key superficial veins:
- Arm: the **cephalic vein** runs up the thumb side, and the **basilic vein** runs up the little-finger side. The **median cubital vein** crosses the front of the elbow between them. It is the usual site for drawing blood.
- Leg: the **great saphenous vein**, the longest vein in the body, starts in front of the medial ankle and runs up the inside of the leg to join the femoral vein in the groin. The **small saphenous vein** runs up the back of the calf to join the popliteal vein behind the knee.

Veins have **valves**, and most blood in the legs drains from superficial to deep. Calf muscles squeezing the deep veins during walking, the **calf muscle pump**, drives blood toward the heart.

Real example: when leg valves fail, superficial veins stretch and twist into **varicose veins**. A clot in a deep vein, called **deep vein thrombosis (DVT)**, is more dangerous because pieces can travel to the lungs.
levels.college:
Limb venous return depends on low-pressure vessels, valves and external pumps. The anatomy has three parts: superficial veins in the subcutaneous tissue, deep veins within the fascial compartments, and perforators connecting them.

**Upper limb**
- The dorsal venous network of the hand drains laterally into the **cephalic vein** and medially into the **basilic vein**.
- The cephalic vein ascends in the deltopectoral groove, pierces the clavipectoral fascia and ends in the **axillary vein**.
- The basilic vein pierces the deep fascia in the mid-arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major.
- The **median cubital vein** links cephalic to basilic in the cubital fossa. It lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which partly shields the brachial artery and median nerve.
- Deep veins are paired **venae comitantes** (radial, ulnar, brachial) that hug their arteries.

**Lower limb**
- The **great saphenous vein (GSV)** passes anterior to the medial malleolus with the saphenous nerve. It ascends medially, about a hand's breadth behind the patella at the knee. At the **saphenofemoral junction** it passes through the saphenous opening, about 3-4 cm inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
- The **small saphenous vein** passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve. It usually ends at the **saphenopopliteal junction**.
- Deep veins: paired tibial and fibular venae comitantes form the **popliteal vein**, which becomes the **femoral vein** at the adductor hiatus. The femoral vein lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle and becomes the external iliac vein deep to the inguinal ligament.
- The calf contains **soleal and gastrocnemial venous sinuses**, the reservoirs of the calf pump.

**Physiology**: Valves are bicuspid and most numerous distally. Perforator valves direct flow from superficial to deep. Calf contraction can generate pressures above 200 mmHg in the deep compartment. Walking lowers ankle venous pressure from about 90 mmHg (standing still) to about 20-30 mmHg. If valves fail, this drop is lost, causing **chronic venous hypertension**.
levels.phd:
Venous return from the limbs is a hemodynamic problem. In the standing adult, the hydrostatic column from right atrium to ankle produces roughly 80-100 mmHg at the foot. Arterial-to-venous pressure gradients alone cannot overcome this without help. The solution is a valved, segmented system plus muscular pumps.

**Valve architecture.** Venous valves are bicuspid endothelial folds with a connective tissue core. They sit in a dilated sinus where flow forms a vortex that washes the valve pocket. Valve density rises distally: the calf and tibial veins carry many valves, while the common femoral and iliac segments have few, often one or none above the saphenofemoral junction. The valve sinus has relatively low shear and is relatively hypoxic. This makes it a favored site for thrombus initiation, which fits with **Virchow's triad** (stasis, endothelial change, hypercoagulability).

**Pump hierarchy.** Plantar venous plexus compression during weight bearing, the calf pump (gastrocnemius-soleus acting on soleal sinuses within the tight crural fascia) and the thigh pump work in series. The calf pump ejects a large fraction of calf venous volume per contraction. **Ambulatory venous pressure** (AVP), measured in a dorsal foot vein during tiptoe exercise, quantifies pump performance. AVP and refill time correlate with ulcer risk in chronic venous disease.

**Perforators** number over 100 per leg. Named clinically important groups include the medial calf (Cockett, now called posterior tibial perforators), paratibial and mid-thigh (Hunterian/Dodd) perforators. Many medial calf perforators connect to the **posterior arch vein** rather than the GSV trunk itself. Failure causes outward "blowout" of high calf pressures into the subcutaneous tissues of the gaiter region.

**Saphenous compartment.** Duplex ultrasound shows the GSV lying within a fascial sheath, the "Egyptian eye" image. This distinguishes the true saphenous trunk from superficial accessory and tributary veins. The distinction underpins modern classification of reflux.

**Pathogenesis debate.** The classical view holds that primary valve failure progresses upward from the junction (descending theory). Duplex studies show that reflux often begins in tributaries or segmentally and spreads upward (ascending/multifocal theory). Vein wall remodeling, with altered matrix metalloproteinase activity and smooth-muscle disorganization, may come before valve incompetence. Leukocyte trapping and inflammation drive skin changes such as lipodermatosclerosis.
levels.expert:
Clinically, venous anatomy matters most in four arenas: access, thrombosis, reflux surgery and conduit harvest.

**Access.** The cephalic vein at the wrist is the classic outflow for a radiocephalic (Brescia-Cimino) arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis. Patients likely to need dialysis should have that arm's veins spared from routine cannulation. At the antecubital fossa, the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve accompanies the cephalic side and the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve the basilic side. The brachial artery lies deep to the bicipital aponeurosis, so deep medial punctures carry the greatest risk. PICC lines are usually placed in the basilic or brachial vein under ultrasound in the upper arm.

**Thrombosis pitfalls.** The "superficial femoral vein" is a deep vein. Calling it superficial has led to untreated proximal DVT, so current nomenclature (Union Internationale de Phlébologie consensus) prefers simply **femoral vein**. Thrombophlebitis of the GSV within about 3 cm of the saphenofemoral junction is generally managed like DVT because of the risk of extension. Isolated calf (distal) DVT management, surveillance versus anticoagulation, remains debated. **May-Thurner** compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery explains the left-sided predominance of iliofemoral DVT. **Paget-Schroetter** syndrome, effort thrombosis of the subclavian-axillary vein, occurs at the costoclavicular space in young athletes.

**Reflux treatment.** Ligation and stripping has largely given way to endovenous thermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency), cyanoacrylate closure and foam sclerotherapy. Junction anatomy dictates technique. The **saphenous nerve** runs with the below-knee GSV, which limits aggressive treatment there. The **sural nerve** has a similar relationship with the small saphenous vein. The saphenopopliteal junction is highly variable, with high or absent terminations and a Giacomini thigh extension, so it is mapped by duplex before intervention. The ESCHAR and EVRA trials found that correcting superficial reflux reduces ulcer recurrence and speeds healing, respectively.

**Conduit.** The GSV remains a key graft for coronary and infrainguinal bypass. Endothelial preservation during harvest (no-touch technique) is an active research area.

Open questions include the triggers of valve failure, deep venous valve reconstruction and stenting outcomes, and imaging biomarkers of post-thrombotic syndrome.

keyPoints: Superficial veins lie in subcutaneous tissue; deep veins run with arteries under deep fascia
Perforating veins link the two systems and normally direct flow from superficial to deep
Arm: cephalic (lateral), basilic (medial), median cubital at the elbow
Leg: great saphenous (medial, to femoral vein) and small saphenous (posterior, to popliteal vein)
Valves plus the calf muscle pump drive venous return against gravity
Valve failure causes varicose veins; deep vein thrombosis can embolize to the lungs

Beneath the deep fascia beside arteries

Carry blood from deep to superficial veins

It lies in the arm rather than in the leg

kidTest.q: What job do veins do?

advancedTest.q: A patient has incompetent medial calf perforators but a normal deep system. What best explains skin damage in the gaiter region?

Arterial blood bypassing capillaries through the perforators
Lymph refluxing into the small saphenous vein
High calf-pump pressures transmitted outward to superficial tissues

advancedTest.q: Why are valve sinuses favored sites for DVT initiation?

They connect directly to arterial branches
They hold the highest wall shear stress in the leg
They have relatively low shear and are relatively hypoxic

That valves are densest in distal veins
That calf contraction raises deep venous pressure
That reflux descends from a failed junction valve

The common fibular nerve crossing it
The sural nerve running beside it

lessons.title: Lymphatic Drainage of the Limbs & Back

levels.kid:
Your body has a hidden set of tiny tubes called **lymph vessels**. They are like little gutters. They collect extra watery fluid that leaks out of your blood and carry it back home.

Along the way, the fluid passes through **lymph nodes**. These are small bean-shaped checkpoints. Inside, germ-fighting cells check the fluid for germs, like guards at a gate.

Fluid from your arm flows to nodes in your armpit. Fluid from your leg flows to nodes in the fold at the top of your thigh, near your belly. That is why those spots can get sore and swollen when you have a cut or an infection.

If the gutters get blocked, fluid builds up and the arm or leg puffs up.
levels.hs:
Blood capillaries leak fluid into the tissues. Most of it returns to the blood directly, but some does not. The **lymphatic system** collects this extra fluid, now called **lymph**, and returns it to the veins near the heart. On the way, lymph is filtered through **lymph nodes**, where immune cells (lymphocytes) detect germs and cancer cells.

Lymph vessels in the limbs come in two layers:
- **Superficial vessels** run in the fat under the skin and tend to follow the superficial veins.
- **Deep vessels** follow the deep arteries and veins.

The key node groups are:
- **Axillary nodes** in the armpit drain almost the whole upper limb, plus the chest wall and most of the breast.
- **Inguinal nodes** in the groin drain almost the whole lower limb, plus the lower abdominal wall, buttock, and external genitalia.
- The **back** drains by a watershed: skin above the waist goes to the axillary nodes, and skin below the waist goes to the inguinal nodes.

Real example: a child steps on a splinter, and a day later a tender lump appears in the groin. The superficial inguinal nodes are reacting to bacteria carried up from the foot. If lymph flow is blocked, for example after nodes are removed during cancer surgery, fluid collects and the limb swells. This is called **lymphedema**.
levels.college:
Lymph from the limbs moves centripetally through valved vessels. It is propelled by contraction of the vessel walls, by the squeezing of nearby muscles, and by arterial pulsation. It passes through regional node groups before entering the venous system at the **venous angles**, where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet. The left side receives the **thoracic duct** and the right side receives the **right lymphatic duct**.

**Upper limb**
- Superficial vessels from the medial hand and forearm follow the **basilic vein**. Some end in the **cubital (supratrochlear) nodes** just above the medial epicondyle, then continue to the lateral axillary nodes.
- Vessels following the **cephalic vein** can bypass the axilla, running through the deltopectoral groove to the **apical (infraclavicular) nodes**.
- The **axillary nodes** form five groups: humeral (lateral), pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), central, and apical. Flow generally runs peripheral groups → central → apical → **subclavian trunk**.

**Lower limb**
- Superficial vessels follow the **great saphenous vein** to the **superficial inguinal nodes**. These lie in a horizontal group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical group along the terminal great saphenous vein.
- Vessels from the lateral foot and posterolateral calf follow the **small saphenous vein** to the **popliteal nodes**.
- Deep vessels reach the **deep inguinal nodes**, which lie medial to the femoral vein. The most superior of these, in the femoral canal, is often called **Cloquet's node**. Drainage then continues to the external iliac → common iliac → lumbar (lateral aortic) nodes → **cisterna chyli**.

**Back**
- Skin and subcutaneous tissue above roughly the level of the umbilicus or iliac crests drain to the axillary nodes. Below this line, they drain to the superficial inguinal nodes.
- Deep back muscles drain mainly to nodes along the posterior intercostal spaces and the lumbar nodes.

Clinically, a tender node points back to the territory it drains.
levels.phd:
Initial (capillary) lymphatics are blind-ended tubes of oak-leaf endothelial cells joined by discontinuous **button-like junctions**. **Anchoring filaments** made of fibrillin tether them to the extracellular matrix. When interstitial pressure rises, these filaments pull the overlapping cell flaps open, creating primary valves. Pre-collectors lead to **collecting lymphatics**. These are divided into **lymphangions**, segments bounded by bicuspid valves and wrapped in specialized muscle cells. The lymphangions contract in a phasic rhythm, often several times per minute at rest, and nitric oxide and stretch tune the rate. This intrinsic pump does much of the work in the limbs, with skeletal muscle compression adding to it.

Developmentally, lymphatic endothelium buds from the cardinal veins under the control of **PROX1**. Sprouting depends on **VEGF-C** acting on **VEGFR-3** (FLT4), with CCBE1 and ADAMTS3 needed to process VEGF-C into its active form. Mutations explain hereditary lymphedemas:
- **FLT4** mutations cause Milroy disease, which is congenital.
- **FOXC2** mutations cause lymphedema-distichiasis, a defect of the lymphatic valves.
- GATA2 and PIEZO1 mutations cause other inherited forms.

Anatomically, Sappey's classic nineteenth-century mercury-injection studies mapped skin drainage and the truncal watersheds. Later, Kubik described **lymphosomes**, which are territories drained by specific collector bundles. These parallel Taylor's angiosomes, but they are not identical to them. Watersheds are not absolute. Collectors can cross the midline and the transverse watershed, especially when the main route is blocked. This variability matters for **melanoma of the back**, which may drain unpredictably to both axillae, both groins, or the neck.

In breast and arm surgery, **reverse lymphatic mapping** showed that the arm's main drainage enters lateral axillary nodes close to the axillary vein. This explains why clearing level I–II nodes disrupts arm lymph flow.

Pathophysiology of chronic lymphedema goes beyond a simple plumbing failure. Stagnant, protein-rich lymph drives CD4+ Th2 inflammation, TGF-β1–mediated fibrosis, and adipocyte hypertrophy. These changes explain why late-stage lymphedema becomes non-pitting and resists compression. Lymphatic filariasis, caused by *Wuchereria bancrofti* and spread by mosquitoes, remains the leading cause of lymphedema worldwide.
levels.expert:
**Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB)** puts limb lymphatic anatomy at the center of oncologic staging. A radiocolloid (for example technetium-99m sulfur colloid or tilmanocept) and/or blue dye or indocyanine green is injected around the primary tumour. Lymphoscintigraphy then identifies the first-echelon node or nodes. Several points matter in practice:
- **Trunk melanomas** drain to an unexpected basin in a meaningful minority of cases, so preoperative imaging is essential.
- Distal limb melanomas can drain to **interval or in-transit nodes**, such as the popliteal or epitrochlear nodes, which surgeons must not overlook.
- MSLT-II (2017) showed that completion lymph node dissection after a positive sentinel node did not improve melanoma-specific survival. Nodal ultrasound surveillance has largely replaced routine groin and axillary clearance, and this spares many patients lymphedema.

The **inguinofemoral dissection** remains highly morbid. Wound breakdown, seroma, and lymphedema are common. Sartorius transposition and saphenous-sparing techniques help reduce these complications.

**Diagnosis of lymphedema.** ICG lymphography stages the disease by dermal backflow patterns, such as the MD Anderson and Arm Dermal Backflow (ADB) scales. It reveals dysfunction before visible swelling appears. Bioimpedance spectroscopy (the L-Dex score) detects subclinical extracellular fluid. Prospective surveillance with early compression may reduce progression after breast surgery, although trial results differ. Lymphoscintigraphy remains the reference functional test. Clinicians should also check for **Stemmer's sign**, which is an inability to pinch the skin fold at the base of the second toe.

**Surgical frontiers**
- **Lymphaticovenular anastomosis (LVA)** is supermicrosurgery that bypasses obstructed lymphatics into subdermal venules. It works best in early, fluid-predominant disease.
- **Vascularized lymph node transfer** uses donor nodes from the groin, submental, omental, or supraclavicular region. Donor-site lymphedema is a feared risk, so reverse mapping is used to protect the donor limb.
- **Liposuction** removes the fatty tissue that dominates late-stage disease, followed by lifelong compression.
- **Immediate lymphatic reconstruction (LYMPHA)** performed at the time of axillary dissection appears to lower lymphedema rates.

**Pitfalls**
- Misreading cellulitis versus deep vein thrombosis in a swollen limb.
- Missing secondary lymphedema caused by recurrent tumour.
- Overlooking lipedema, which is a bilateral, painful fat disorder that spares the feet.

**Open questions** include pharmacological lymphangiogenesis (for example VEGF-C gene therapy), anti-inflammatory and antifibrotic drugs that target the Th2/TGF-β axis, and better prediction of which patients will develop lymphedema.

keyPoints: Lymphatics return leaked tissue fluid to the veins at the venous angles
Axillary nodes drain nearly all of the upper limb
Inguinal nodes drain nearly all of the lower limb
Back skin drains to the axilla above the umbilical watershed and to the groin below it
Popliteal and cubital nodes are small distal relay stations
Blocked lymph flow causes lymphedema; sentinel node biopsy uses this drainage map

Sentinel node biopsy became unnecessary for melanoma staging

lessons.title: Fascial Compartments & Compartment Syndrome

levels.kid:
Inside your arms and legs, muscles are packed into bags made of tough, stretchy-but-not-very-stretchy wrapping. This wrapping is called **fascia**. Each bag is a **compartment**.

Imagine stuffing too many socks into a small drawer. The drawer can't get bigger, so everything inside gets squashed.

If a leg gets badly hurt, the muscles can swell. The fascia bag doesn't stretch, so the pressure inside goes way up. That squeezes the blood vessels and nerves, and the muscle can't get the blood it needs. This is called **compartment syndrome**.

The big clue is pain that is much worse than it should be. Doctors fix it fast by carefully opening the bag to let the pressure out.
levels.hs:
Your limbs are divided into **fascial compartments**: groups of muscles, along with their nerves and blood vessels, wrapped by **deep fascia** and walls of fascia called **intermuscular septa**. Muscles in one compartment usually share a job and a nerve supply. For example, the leg below the knee has four compartments: **anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior**.

Fascia is strong but barely stretches. That makes compartments useful (they hold muscles in place and help pump venous blood back up), but also risky.

**Compartment syndrome** happens when pressure inside a closed compartment rises high enough to block blood flow to the tissues. Common causes:
- Fractures, especially of the **tibia** (shin bone)
- Crush injuries
- Blood flow returning after a blocked artery is reopened
- Tight casts or bandages

As pressure rises, small veins collapse first, so fluid builds up and pressure climbs even more: a vicious cycle. Nerves and muscles start to die from lack of oxygen within hours.

The earliest and most important sign is **pain out of proportion** to the injury, especially pain when the muscles in that compartment are passively stretched. The emergency treatment is a **fasciotomy**: surgeons cut the fascia open to release the pressure. Real example: a motorcyclist with a broken tibia whose pain keeps getting worse despite strong painkillers needs urgent assessment.
levels.college:
**Compartment anatomy.** Deep fascia and intermuscular septa partition limbs into compartments whose muscles generally share function and innervation:
- **Arm**: anterior (flexors, musculocutaneous n.) and posterior (triceps, radial n.).
- **Forearm**: volar/flexor, dorsal/extensor, and the **mobile wad** (brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis). The flexor compartment is most often affected.
- **Hand**: ten compartments (thenar, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, central, four dorsal and three palmar interossei groups; counts vary by source).
- **Thigh**: anterior (femoral n.), medial (obturator n.), posterior (sciatic n.).
- **Leg**: anterior (deep fibular n., anterior tibial a.), lateral (superficial fibular n.), superficial posterior (soleus, gastrocnemius), deep posterior (tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus; tibial n., posterior tibial and fibular aa.).
- **Gluteal** and **foot** compartments also exist.

**Pathophysiology.** Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) follows when compartment pressure rises toward capillary and venous pressure. Venous outflow collapses, the arteriovenous gradient falls, and capillary perfusion fails even though the large artery, and so the distal pulse, may persist. Ischemia increases capillary leak and edema, raising pressure further. Muscle tolerates roughly 4-6 hours of ischemia before irreversible necrosis begins; nerve function is lost sooner.

**Diagnosis.** It is mainly clinical. Pain out of proportion and pain on **passive stretch** are earliest. Paresthesia follows (e.g., numbness in the first dorsal web space with anterior leg ACS, from deep fibular nerve compression). Pallor, paralysis and pulselessness are **late**. Pressure measurement supports diagnosis: **delta pressure** (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg or less is a common fasciotomy threshold.

**Treatment.** Remove constricting dressings, keep the limb at heart level (elevation reduces arterial inflow), and perform urgent fasciotomy. In the leg, a **two-incision technique** releases all four compartments.

**Complications.** Untreated ACS causes muscle necrosis, **rhabdomyolysis** with myoglobinuric kidney injury, and **Volkmann ischemic contracture**.
levels.phd:
**Physiological basis.** The arteriovenous gradient theory (Matsen) frames ACS as loss of local perfusion: tissue perfusion is proportional to (Pa - Pv)/R, and because thin-walled veins cannot remain open below tissue pressure, venous pressure rises with compartment pressure. Rising compartment pressure therefore shrinks the gradient until microvascular flow ceases, long before systemic arterial pressure is exceeded. This explains why distal pulses and capillary refill can be normal in established ACS, and why hypotension lowers the pressure tolerated.

**Thresholds.** Normal resting intracompartmental pressure is near 0-8 mmHg. Early fixed thresholds (30 or 45 mmHg) were replaced after Whitesides (1975) proposed perfusion-relative criteria, later refined by McQueen and Court-Brown (1996): a **ΔP** (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg identified ACS while avoiding many unnecessary fasciotomies in tibial fractures with high absolute pressures. Diastolic pressure is used as the conservative estimate of perfusion pressure, but intraoperative anesthesia lowers it, so comparing against preoperative values remains debated.

**Cellular injury.** Ischemia depletes ATP and causes Na+/K+-ATPase failure, cellular swelling, Ca2+ overload, and activation of phospholipases and calpains. **Reperfusion** generates reactive oxygen species (xanthine oxidase, neutrophil NADPH oxidase), increasing endothelial permeability; this is why ACS often appears after revascularization. Muscle necrosis releases myoglobin, K+ and H+, driving acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia and acidosis.

**Regional vulnerability.** The anterior leg compartment is most frequently involved: it is tightly bounded by tibia, fibula, interosseous membrane and dense crural fascia. The deep posterior compartment is the most commonly missed at fasciotomy. In the forearm, deep flexors (flexor digitorum profundus, flexor pollicis longus) lie closest to the bone and the anterior interosseous artery, and are hit first. This is why **Volkmann contracture** classically affects them after supracondylar humeral fractures in children.

**Variants.** **Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS)** produces reversible, exercise-induced pressure rises with pain that resolves at rest, usually in the anterior/lateral leg of runners and military recruits. Diagnosis traditionally used Pedowitz criteria, whose specificity has been criticized.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls.** The clinical signs of ACS are individually poor: pain and pain on passive stretch have high negative predictive value but low positive predictive value. The classic "5 Ps" teaching misleads trainees, because pulselessness usually signals arterial injury, not ACS. High-risk patients in whom examination fails include the obtunded or intubated, children (the "3 As": increasing **analgesic** need, **anxiety**, **agitation**), patients with regional nerve blocks or patient-controlled analgesia, and those with concurrent nerve injury. In these groups, serial or continuous pressure monitoring carries more weight. Single readings vary with catheter position, so measure within about 5 cm of the fracture and check every compartment at risk.

**Non-fracture causes.** ACS can develop without a fracture: anticoagulated soft-tissue bleeding, prolonged immobilization (the lithotomy position, or after being found down), burns with circumferential eschar (treated by escharotomy), IV extravasation, snakebite envenomation, and reperfusion after vascular repair. After revascularization of prolonged limb ischemia, vascular surgeons often perform **prophylactic fasciotomy**. Envenomation is a notable exception: antivenom is first-line, because true ACS there is uncommon and fasciotomy can worsen outcomes.

**Late presentation.** Fasciotomy of a compartment already necrotic for well over a day converts a closed injury into an open, infected one and raises amputation and sepsis risk. Many authors therefore advise against routine late fasciotomy and manage the established necrosis and its systemic effects instead. This judgment carries much of the medicolegal risk in orthopedics, where missed ACS is a leading source of litigation.

**Operative details.** In the two-incision leg fasciotomy, the anterolateral incision releases the anterior and lateral compartments and must protect the **superficial fibular nerve** as it pierces the fascia. The posteromedial incision releases the superficial posterior compartment, then detaches soleus from the tibia to reach the deep posterior compartment. Wounds are closed in a delayed fashion or skin-grafted; negative-pressure dressings are widely used.

**Frontiers.** Researchers are working toward objective, continuous diagnosis:
- **Near-infrared spectroscopy** to track tissue oxygenation
- Intramuscular pH and glucose probes
- Wireless pressure sensors

Most of this work is in validation studies. For CECS, surgical fasciotomy is the established treatment, but gait retraining (forefoot strike) and botulinum toxin injection are being studied as nonsurgical options. A neurosurgery-minded reader should also note that nerve ischemia in compartments can leave permanent deficits even when muscle survives.

keyPoints: Deep fascia and septa divide limbs into compartments sharing function and nerve supply
The leg has four compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial and deep posterior
Rising pressure collapses veins first and destroys the arteriovenous perfusion gradient
Earliest signs: pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch; pulses often persist
Delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) of 30 mmHg or less supports fasciotomy
Untreated ACS causes necrosis, rhabdomyolysis and Volkmann contracture

test.q: How many fascial compartments are in the leg below the knee?
test.explain: The leg has anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior compartments.

test.q: What is usually the earliest sign of acute compartment syndrome?
choices: Paralysis of muscles in the limb
Pale, cool skin over the limb
Pain out of proportion to injury
Loss of the pulse below the injury
test.explain: Disproportionate pain, especially on passive stretch, comes first. Pulselessness, pallor and paralysis are late.

test.q: Which fracture is most commonly linked to acute compartment syndrome?
test.explain: Tibial fractures are the classic cause, especially affecting the anterior leg compartment.

test.q: Why can a distal pulse remain present in compartment syndrome?
choices: Collateral veins carry oxygen to the muscle
Large arteries keep flowing while capillary perfusion fails
The nerve keeps the artery dilated during swelling
The fascia stretches to protect the main artery
test.explain: Compartment pressure blocks microvascular flow well below systemic arterial pressure, so the large artery and its pulse can persist.

test.q: The definitive treatment for acute compartment syndrome is:
test.explain: Fasciotomy opens the fascia to relieve pressure. Elevation can reduce arterial inflow and should be avoided.

test.q: Which nerve travels in the anterior compartment of the leg?
test.explain: The deep fibular nerve runs with the anterior tibial artery. Its compression causes numbness in the first dorsal web space.

test.q: Delta pressure is calculated as:
choices: Mean arterial pressure minus heart rate
test.explain: A delta pressure of 30 mmHg or less is a common threshold for fasciotomy.

test.q: Which compartment of the thigh is supplied by the obturator nerve?
test.explain: The medial (adductor) compartment is innervated by the obturator nerve, the anterior by the femoral and the posterior by the sciatic.

test.q: Muscle breakdown from untreated compartment syndrome can injure the kidneys through:
test.explain: Necrotic muscle releases myoglobin, which can cause acute kidney injury.

test.q: Walls of fascia between muscle groups are called intermuscular ___.
test.explain: Intermuscular septa, together with deep fascia, form the walls of compartments.

test.q: What is the name of the flexion contracture of the forearm caused by untreated compartment ischemia?
test.explain: Volkmann ischemic contracture follows necrosis of the deep forearm flexors.

test.q: Pain on passive ___ of the compartment's muscles is an early sign of compartment syndrome.
test.explain: Stretching ischemic muscles increases the pain sharply.

kidTest.q: What is fascia?
choices: A small bone inside the leg
A tiny type of blood cell
kidTest.explain: Fascia wraps muscles into bags called compartments.

kidTest.q: Why does pressure go up when muscle swells?
kidTest.explain: The fascia bag can't get bigger, so swelling squeezes everything inside.

kidTest.q: What is a big clue of compartment syndrome?
choices: A sleepy feeling in the evening
kidTest.explain: Pain that is far too strong for the injury is the key warning sign.

kidTest.q: How do doctors fix it?
choices: By giving the person a snack
kidTest.explain: Opening the fascia lets the pressure out so blood can flow again.

kidTest.q: Each fascia bag of muscles is called a c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Muscles sit in fascia bags called compartments.

advancedTest.q: Why does systemic hypotension make a patient more vulnerable to compartment syndrome at a given compartment pressure?
choices: Low blood pressure stiffens the fascia and raises tissue pressure further
Hypotension directly damages peripheral nerves within the compartment
A lower diastolic pressure narrows the gradient driving capillary perfusion
Low pressure raises venous outflow and drains the compartment too quickly
advancedTest.explain: Perfusion depends on arterial pressure relative to tissue pressure. Lower diastolic pressure reduces delta pressure, so ischemia occurs at lower compartment pressures.

advancedTest.q: A tibial fracture patient has a compartment pressure of 40 mmHg with a diastolic BP of 85 mmHg. What does a perfusion-based approach suggest?
choices: Amputation, because the pressure shows the muscle has died
Elevate the limb well above the heart to reduce the swelling
Immediate fasciotomy, because the pressure exceeds a fixed 30 mmHg cutoff
Fasciotomy is not mandated yet; delta pressure is 45 mmHg, so monitor closely
advancedTest.explain: Delta pressure (85 - 40 = 45) is above 30 mmHg. McQueen's criteria avoid unnecessary fasciotomies based on absolute pressure alone.

advancedTest.q: Why is routine fasciotomy often discouraged when compartment syndrome is discovered after well over a day?
choices: The nerves have fully regenerated by then, so release brings no benefit
Compartment pressure returns to normal on its own within a few hours
Opening necrotic muscle adds infection risk without saving tissue
Fascia has thickened by then and is far too tough to cut through safely
advancedTest.explain: Established necrosis can't be rescued, and opening it converts a closed injury into an open, infection-prone one.

advancedTest.q: Why is acute compartment syndrome a recognized risk after revascularizing a limb with prolonged ischemia?
choices: Reperfusion generates oxidants that increase capillary leak and edema
Revascularization lowers venous pressure and pulls fluid into the bone
Restored arterial flow cools the tissue and causes spasm of the fascia
The bypass graft compresses the compartment from outside the fascia
advancedTest.explain: Reactive oxygen species formed during reperfusion damage the endothelium. The resulting edema raises compartment pressure, which is why prophylactic fasciotomy is often done.
